newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: ABARE sees top Australian winter and summer crops.
newsitem.headline: ABARE sees top Australian winter and summer crops.

text.p: Recent rain in eastern Australia is likely result in winter crop plantings equal to last year's 18 million hectares, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said on Tuesday.
ABARE's latest Australian Crop Report, released on Tuesday, puts Australia's total 1997/98 winter crop area at 18.25 million hectares, down marginally from 18.30 million in 1996/97.
The forecast is up from ABARE's previous forecast for the current winter crop, issued in February, of 17.35 million ha.

"Despite recent planting rains, there are still concerns about follow-up winter rainfall, with some seasonal indicators being less than favourable," ABARE actubg executive director Stephen Beare said in a statement accompanying the report.
"While rainfall has been below average in the eastern states, it is still a little early to be predicting an El Nino event (dry weather associated with sea temperatures)," he said.
While planting of wheat and barley was expected to be slightly lower than the year before, plantings of oilseeds and pulses were likely to increase markedly, Beare said.

The increased pulse and oilseed plantings reflected the availability of new varieties and a shift in relative gross margins. The canola area alone was expected to increase by more than 70 percent to 650,000 hectares, he said.
The area planted to wheat was forecast to remain high at more than 11 million hectares, only slightly down on last year.
Sowings were expected to expand in Queensland, with central Queensland experiencing the best start to the winter crop season for a number of years, he said.

The summer crop was not expected to be completed until July, but total summer crop production in 1996/97 was estimated at a record four million tonnes, about seven percent higher than the previous record crop in 1991/92, he said.
This was underpinned by record cotton and rice crops in 1996/97, he said.

"With winter and summer crop production records, 1996/97 is expected to set a new total crop production record of 39.2 million tonnes, 18 percent higher than the previous record set in 1983/84," Beare said.

Good falls of rain in the cropping regions of New South Wales (NSW) and Queensland in mid to late May had alleviated some of the concerns caused by near-record dry conditions across eastern Australia in March and April, ABARE's report said.
A major factor contributing to high winter crop plantings was the expectation of high returns for grains, oilseeds and pulses in 1997/98 relative to forecast returns for wool and beef, it said.
Reflecting this, closing sheep numbers were expected to remain low at about 124 million in 1997/98, it said.
ABARE said the area sown to all other winter cereals was expected to decline in 1997/98 but the largest fall was expected in barley, down by 129,000 hectares to about 3.1 million.

In contrast, areas sown to oilseeds and pulses in 1997/98 are forecast to set new records. Oilseeds' area is forecast to increase by 70 percent to 700,000 ha, mainly reflecting increased canola plantings in all states, it said.
Oilseed production in 1996/97 is forecast to increase to 1.16 million tonnes from 797,000 tonnes the year before.

Pulses sown area for 1997/98 is forecast at a record 2.02 million ha, up from 1.90 million ha in the year before, mainly because of increased lupin plantings in Western Australia and lentil plantings in Victoria. Pulses production for 1996/97 is forecast at 35,000 tonnes, up from 24,000 the year before.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
